strengths: Principled taxonomy-driven dataset curation addressing previously overlooked perspective-taking capabilities; SenseNova-SI-8M (8.5M QA pairs) systematically combines existing data with 4.5M strategically generated samples

Comprehensive empirical validation across five spatial benchmarks (VSI, MMSI, MindCube, ViewSpatial, SITE), multiple model families (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel), and model sizes demonstrating consistent improvements

Rigorous robustness analysis including circular tests (10-point drop vs. 30+ for baselines), VSI-Debiased evaluation, no-vision ablations (85.6%→52.5% drop), and frame extrapolation (trained on 16 frames, generalizes to 32+) providing strong evidence of genuine spatial reasoning
Broad model scope showing generalization across diverse architectures and pretraining paradigms; downstream validation on embodied AI tasks (EmbodiedBench) demonstrates practical applicability
Clear presentation with effective visualizations; commitment to open-source release of models and code benefits community reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: work is primarily data-centric scaling without introducing new architectures, training techniques, or reasoning mechanisms; core approach is straightforward dataset curation + training existing models

Performance saturation without forward direction: Figure 1 shows clear diminishing returns; authors acknowledge 'data scaling alone is unlikely to achieve human-level' performance and that paradigm shifts are needed, but provide no concrete proposals

Chain-of-Thought analysis disappointing (Section 5.6): all three CoT variants yield only ~2% typical gains, with best variant improving only 8.6% on specific subset; acknowledged as insufficient to justify computational overhead, suggesting text-based reasoning fundamentally limited for spatial understanding

Critical ablation studies missing: no analysis of data balance between dominant capabilities (MM/SR) vs. underrepresented (PT/MR); no component-wise evaluation showing which capabilities drive improvements; no source-level contribution analysis

Perspective-taking (PT) improvements unconvincing: despite positioning PT as critical, ViewSpatial benchmark (PT-focused) achieves only 54.6% vs. 68.7% on broader VSI-Bench; 13.1% gap suggests PT remains significantly harder, contradicting claims of targeted improvement

Data generation quality inadequately documented: 4.5M synthetic samples lack quality metrics, inter-annotator agreement scores, or detailed generation procedures; potential biases in 3D source datasets (ScanNet, Matterport3D) not discussed

Emergent capabilities claims under-supported: 'spill-over' (Fig. 3) based on two anecdotal examples without systematic ablation; 'extrapolation' interesting but not unprecedented and may reflect encoder properties rather than true emergent reasoning

Incomplete baseline comparisons: concurrent works (VST, Cambrian-S) marked with † use cited results rather than reproductions; comparison with proprietary models not under authors' control makes attribution difficult
Statistical rigor lacking: formal significance tests absent despite varied improvement magnitudes (0.72% to 154.4%); confidence bands shown but p-values not provided for critical claims
Manuscript status unclear: abstract states 'this report will be updated continuously,' suggesting evolving work rather than finished submission inappropriate for formal venue

Limited theoretical insight: lacks analysis of why spatial intelligence benefits from data scaling, relationships between spatial capabilities, or fundamental limits of scaling approaches; no investigation into why CoT approaches fail
Narrow evaluation scope: all evaluation on indoor scenes and object manipulation; generalization to outdoor navigation, large-scale environments, or other spatial domains unexplored
Training details sparse: single epoch mentioned without justification; data sampling strategy (balanced vs. natural) unclear; sensitivity to data composition unexplored

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: spatial reasoning deficits in current multimodal models, which is critical for embodied AI applications
Comprehensive data curation effort with 8M samples organized under a principled taxonomy; specifically addresses the previously overlooked perspective-taking capability with 4.5M new samples

Broad empirical evaluation across five spatial benchmarks (VSI-Bench, MMSI, MindCube, ViewSpatial, SITE) and three different base model families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3, Bagel), demonstrating broad applicability

Rigorous robustness analysis convincingly demonstrates genuine spatial reasoning rather than exploitation of shortcuts: circular tests, no-vision evaluations, and bias-debiased benchmarks all show the models learn visual grounding
Interesting observations on emergent capabilities: extrapolation beyond training context (16→32+ frames) and transfer learning between related spatial tasks suggest meta-task structure
Commitment to releasing model weights reduces reproduction costs and benefits the community
Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on tested spatial benchmarks and outperforms GPT-5 on perspective-taking tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The contribution is primarily data engineering using existing architectures without modifications, no novel training procedures, loss functions, or architectural innovations. For CVPR, this is a significant limitation given typical expectations for methodological contributions

Core finding is intuitive and unsurprising: That scaling data on a relevant task improves performance is well-established in the literature. The paper validates an expected outcome rather than discovering novel principles

Saturation and limited path forward: The paper acknowledges diminishing returns and concludes 'data scaling alone is unlikely to achieve human-level spatial intelligence,' which undermines the contribution's long-term value and leaves no clear direction for future work

Insufficient data quality documentation: Minimal details on quality control for 4.5M synthetic samples, no inter-annotator agreement, no human evaluation of generated QA pairs, and no ablation on data quality vs. quantity. This is critical for a data-centric contribution

Concurrent work achieves comparable results: VST [53] and Cambrian-S [54] with similar or less training data achieve comparable performance (VST: 60.6% on VSI-Bench vs. SenseNova-SI 68.7%), raising questions about whether the improvement justifies the data engineering effort

Weak chain-of-thought analysis: Section 5.6 shows CoT variants provide only marginal ~2% gains, contradicting the emphasis on this direction. Claims about needing 'different reasoning mechanisms' are preliminary and underdeveloped

Questionable emergence claims: Evidence for 'emergent generalization' is somewhat anecdotal—single-dataset training/testing (Section 5.4.1) doesn't thoroughly probe emergence; extrapolation to 32 frames is modest; claims are overstated relative to evidence

Architectural constraints: Deliberate avoidance of modifying base architectures limits potential gains and leaves unclear whether architectural innovations could better address spatial reasoning. The paper essentially performs continued pretraining without exploration of better inductive biases

Benchmark concerns: Concurrent benchmarks (VSI, MMSI, etc. all 2025) may have data overlap with training sources (ScanNet, Ego-Exo4D). No explicit contamination checks reported; raises fairness questions in comparisons

Missing critical ablations: No ablation on contribution of different dataset sources, no comparison with alternative data augmentation strategies, no analysis of which data combinations are most impactful

Limited generalization validation: General multimodal performance on MMBench-En actually drops (-1.30% for Qwen3-VL-8B); claims of capability preservation shown on only one benchmark. How does it perform on VQA, GQA, and other general tasks?
Insufficient methodological justification: Training for only 1 epoch, very low learning rate (5×10^-6), massive batch size (2048)—no justification or ablation studies on these choices
Reproducibility gaps: While model weights will be released, data curation process insufficiently documented; prompts for synthetic data generation not provided; 3D dataset processing details sparse

Philosophical limitation: Paper addresses 'if we train on spatial data, do we get spatial reasoning?' but doesn't address *why* models struggle with spatial reasoning. Is it architectural or fundamentally a data problem? No deeper insights provided
Limited downstream validation: Only embodied manipulation evaluated; improvements on EmbodiedBench not contextualized against other approaches; no comparison with specialized embodied AI models
Missing error analysis: No characterization of remaining failure modes; no analysis of which spatial capabilities remain most challenging; limits insights into fundamental limitations

Presentation issues: Paper describes itself as 'ongoing project' to be 'updated continuously'—unusual for conference submission. Figure 1 overcrowded and difficult to parse. Vague claims like 'unprecedented performance'

strengths: Systematic and principled approach to dataset construction using the EASI taxonomy, addressing previously overlooked perspective-taking (PT) capabilities across five coherent spatial dimensions

Impressive empirical results across five spatial intelligence benchmarks (VSI-Bench: 68.7%, MMSI: 43.3%, MindCube: 85.6%, ViewSpatial: 54.6%, SITE: 50.1%) while maintaining strong general multimodal performance (MMBench-En: 84.9%), with consistent improvements across multiple base model architectures

Rigorous robustness validation through multiple complementary approaches: circular tests, no-vision evaluation, VSI-Debiased testing, and controlled single-source experiments demonstrating genuine spatial reasoning rather than shortcuts or language priors

Comprehensive empirical analysis including scaling laws, capability emergence (spill-over effects, frame extrapolation), and honest examination of limitations (saturation, minimal CoT gains), providing valuable insights for future research

Substantial resource contribution with commitment to publicly release 8.5M curated samples and trained models across three foundation model families, addressing data scarcity in spatial intelligence research
Evaluation on downstream embodied AI task (EmbodiedBench) without finetuning demonstrates practical utility and 60% improvement over base models
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and consistent results across different model sizes and architectures
weaknesses: Limited technical and methodological novelty: the core contribution is data-centric scaling of existing models without architectural innovations or novel training paradigms. The approach is essentially 'collect data, fine-tune base models,' which is incremental for a top-tier venue

Saturation trends in scaling curves (Figure 1) show diminishing returns, suggesting that data scaling alone may have reached practical limits. The paper acknowledges this but provides limited insights into overcoming these barriers, limiting future impact potential

Chain-of-thought analysis (Section 5.6) yields disappointing results—all three CoT variants produce only marginal ~2% gains, underperforming simple QA-style training. This negative result suggests limitations in reasoning capabilities and paradigmatic constraints

Insufficient discussion of data contamination risks: while the paper incorporates 3.3M existing spatial dataset samples plus 4.5M synthetically generated samples, potential overlap with test benchmarks is not thoroughly addressed. No explicit train/test validation procedures are described

Limited analysis of data quality for the 4.5M newly synthetic samples: The paper lacks details on annotation validation, quality assurance metrics, or human evaluation of the synthetic QA generation process from 3D datasets

Incomplete experimental comparisons: reliance on reported results from concurrent works (VST, Cambrian-S) rather than author-verified results. Performance margins over some baselines are modest and lack statistical significance testing

Minimal failure case and error analysis: The paper does not provide qualitative examination of where models still fail or which spatial reasoning types remain challenging, limiting insights into fundamental limitations

Benchmark domain similarity concerns: Several training datasets (CLEVR series, Open3D-VQA) overlap conceptually with test benchmarks. While direct contamination is avoided, domain similarity may inflate results relative to truly novel spatial reasoning capabilities
Limited downstream task evaluation: Only EmbodiedBench spatial subset is tested. Evaluation on diverse embodied AI tasks or actual robotic systems would strengthen practical validity claims

Incomplete reporting for reproducibility: Model and code links are placeholders; some dataset construction details (QA generation procedures, sampling strategies, data ordering) are underspecified; inconsistency between 8M (abstract) and 8.5M (text) QA pairs

Perspective-taking emphasis lacks deep justification: While PT data collection is presented as a key contribution, limited analysis explains why PT was underrepresented or how much the emphasis contributed to improvements relative to other capability dimensions

Generalization claims partially overstated: Capability spill-over (Figure 3) is demonstrated in controlled experiments on specific dataset pairs. Generalization to truly novel tasks is less clear, evidenced by the relatively modest SITE performance (50.1%)

strengths: Systematic and principled data curation addressing key gaps (especially perspective-taking), yielding 8.5M diverse samples organized under a well-motivated cognitive taxonomy
Comprehensive evaluation across five recent spatial benchmarks (VSI, MMSI, MindCube, ViewSpatial, SITE) with strong results competitive with proprietary models and clear ablations/breakdowns
Rigorous robustness analysis including circular tests, no-vision tests, and debiased benchmarks that convincingly demonstrate genuine spatial reasoning rather than language shortcuts
Extensive empirical analysis of scaling laws, emergent generalization (spillover, extrapolation), and cross-architecture validation (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3, Bagel)
Thorough retention of general capabilities (MMBench-En, MMStar, AI2D, OCRBench) showing training on spatial data doesn't cause catastrophic forgetting
Strong commitment to reproducibility with detailed training specs, code/model release, and comprehensive appendices enabling community replication
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: contribution is primarily data-centric (scaling existing models on curated data) with no architectural innovations or new training paradigms; curation practices follow established approaches

Saturation observed without solutions: performance plateaus significantly after ~5-6M samples (Fig. 1, Table 7); paper acknowledges data scaling alone insufficient but offers no path forward; vague claims about 'paradigm shifts' lack substance

Chain-of-Thought results underwhelming: all three CoT variants yield only ~2% gains with 1000-2000+ token overhead; analysis is preliminary with tentative hypotheses rather than insights into why text-based reasoning fails for spatial tasks

Dataset contribution lacks transparency: exact breakdown of 8.5M samples across capabilities missing; inter-annotator agreement, quality metrics for auto-generated QA pairs, and validation procedures not reported; unclear how much improvement stems from existing vs. newly curated data

Emergent capability claims overstated: spillover within perspective-taking is expected transfer; extrapolation from 16→32 frames shows modest gains (~4%) with degradation beyond 64 frames; interesting but incremental findings

Inadequate ablation studies: no direct removal of PT data to quantify its specific contribution; fairness of comparisons unclear (VST/Cambrian-S achieve less improvement with comparable data—why?); cross-dataset transfer not analyzed

Downstream evaluation limited to single task (embodied manipulation) without comparison to other spatial approaches; absolute success rates remain modest (16.6%→33.3%); unclear why this task specifically benefits or how findings generalize

Missing systematic failure analysis: while robustness tests validate visual grounding, analysis of which spatial reasoning types remain hard is absent; Figure 6 c,d failures lack categorization and deeper investigation
Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals or significance tests; standard deviations shown only in radar charts; single training runs without reported variance across seeds

Scope and presentation issues: paper reads as technical report rather than research contribution; framing as 'ongoing project' atypical for CVPR; dense 33-page submission; some vague claims about 'unprecedented performance' require qualification

strengths: Addresses an important gap in spatial intelligence capabilities of multimodal models
Systematic taxonomy-driven data curation approach with rigorous quality control (8M samples, detailed pipeline in Appendix B)
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 major benchmarks with detailed per-benchmark analysis and ablations
Strong robustness validation through circular tests, no-vision experiments, and controlled generalization studies convincingly showing genuine spatial understanding rather than shortcuts
Demonstrated improvements on perspective-taking relative to GPT-5 (80.7% vs 48.6% on VSI Rel. Dir) and competitive results on multiple benchmarks
Valuable commitment to open-source release of models and code for community use
Interesting controlled experiments showing spill-over effects and extrapolation beyond training distribution
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is data scaling without architectural innovations, novel training paradigms, or methodological advances—a well-established approach by 2026 with expected results

Chain-of-Thought experiments (Section 5.6) critically undermine reasoning claims: three CoT variants yield only ~2% improvement despite 100K training examples, with vague post-hoc explanations but no solutions; if text-based reasoning doesn't help, why is data scaling alone sufficient?

Marginal improvements over concurrent work: vs. Cambrian-S-7B, differences are often modest (VSI: 68.7% vs 67.5%, +1.2%; MMSI: 43.3% vs 25.8% but likely due to different data/protocols) with no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Clear saturation in performance (Fig. 1) acknowledged by authors ('data scaling alone unlikely to achieve human-level'), yet no concrete proposed solutions, alternative mechanisms, or viable paths forward are discussed

Data contamination risks not addressed: potential overlap between 8.5M training samples and test benchmarks unknown; ScanNet, ScanNet++, Matterport3D used for QA generation may overlap with benchmark construction; no inter-annotator agreement or quality metrics for generated QAs

Superficial analysis of claimed 'emergent spatial intelligence': (1) spill-over shows only modest transfer within related spatial tasks; (2) extrapolation drops from 68.8% (32 frames) to 66.3% (128 frames), contradicting claimed robust generalization, yet text only highlights improvements

Perspective-taking contribution lacks depth: simply scaling underrepresented PT data is obvious engineering, not novel research; performance remains weak on challenging PT subsets (e.g., ViewSpatial person-based 43.1%); no analysis of why PT is fundamentally difficult

Missing critical ablations: no data composition ablation, data efficiency curves, or analysis of which spatial capabilities contribute most to improvements; unclear whether 8M samples necessary or 4M suffices
Reproducibility concerns: 'Further Scaling' methodology on 3D datasets insufficient detail for reproduction; data filtering thresholds, QA generation validation, and computational costs not specified

General capability degradation under-discussed: AI2D drops 6.2% (85.2%→79.0%), OCRBench drops 65 points (880→815); paper dismisses as 'minimal' despite being substantial; trade-offs between spatial and general understanding not analyzed

Statistical rigor absent: no significance testing, confidence intervals unexplained (±0.5 std dev in Fig. 1 origin unclear), some concurrent baselines use different evaluation protocols; radar chart normalization (worst→0.2, not 0.0) distorts perception

Embodied task evaluation superficial: 16.6% absolute success rate remains very low; discrete table-top action space unrepresentative of embodied AI; no comparison with embodied AI baselines beyond base model; feels like afterthought not integrated validation

Writing as technical report, not research paper: key findings scattered across appendices; insights buried (e.g., CoT limitations); overclaimed statements ('unprecedented performance' for marginal improvements over Cambrian-S)
Error analysis and failure mode taxonomy absent; unclear what spatial reasoning types remain problematic; why GPT-5 underperforms on PT vs. excels on SR not explored

strengths: Systematic, principled approach using EASI taxonomy for decomposing spatial intelligence into core capabilities
Large-scale curated dataset (8M samples) with sophisticated filtering and image selection pipeline
Strong empirical results across 5 diverse benchmarks, surpassing GPT-5 on perspective-taking (80.7% vs lower performance)
Rigorous robustness evaluation including circular tests, VSI-Debiased evaluation, and no-vision controls demonstrating genuine visual grounding
Comprehensive analysis of scaling behaviors, emergent generalization, and single-dataset training necessity
Multi-architecture validation (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel) demonstrating approach generalization
Public commitment to release models, code, and dataset, providing significant community value
Downstream validation on embodied AI without finetuning (+59.6% success rate improvement)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily data-centric scaling without architectural innovation or modifications to base models
Preliminary and inconclusive CoT analysis showing only 2-7% gains; proposed hypotheses are speculative rather than conclusive
Saturation plateau effects (Fig 1) suggest fundamental limitations of scaling-only approaches; paper acknowledges but doesn't address paradigm shift needed
Synthetic data quality control procedures underspecified: validation methodology, error rates, and manual verification extent not reported for 4.5M generated samples
Data contamination prevention not explicitly discussed despite combining diverse multi-source datasets; risk of train-test overlap unclear
Limited failure mode analysis—Section 5.7 shows failures but provides no systematic breakdown or generalizable insights
Generalization concerns: predominantly indoor scene training (ScanNet-based); modest SITE performance (47.7%) suggests distribution specificity
Training setup inadequately justified: single-epoch training rationale unexplained, learning rate arbitrary (5×10⁻⁶), no statistical significance testing or error bars reported
Missing ablations on dataset composition, data mixture sensitivity, and impact of individual spatial capabilities
Dense presentation (33 pages) with normalized radar charts obscuring absolute performance differences; CoT notation inconsistently applied
